Illustration: Nik Spencer/*Nature.* Adapted from image by Accogliente Design/Shutterstock

From the United States to Europe to Brazil, there is a pervasive sense that trust in science has collapsed.

The complex truth about trust in science

In the United States, President Donald Trump and his administration are using the idea that science is not trustworthy as [one reason to cut research budgets](https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-026-00088-9), [reject evidence-based medical advice](https://www.nature.com/articles/d41591-026-00002-w) and exert unprecedented political control over research. “Over the last 5 years, confidence that scientists act in the best interests of the public has fallen significantly,” said Trump in an [executive order last year](https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2025/05/restoring-gold-standard-science/).

Even the Vatican is voicing concern. This September, a meeting at the Pontifical Academy of Sciences will examine how “the crisis of trust in science has become a pressing issue”.

Six ways to put the public at the heart of science and policy

But trust has dropped in certain groups, notably among Republican-leaning people in the United States. And research in the United Kingdom shows that the proportion of people who have “a lot” of trust in science tends to be lower among politically right-leaning groups than those on the left. “Trust in science is politicized and becoming more so,” says sociologist Gordon Gauchat at the University of Wisconsin–Milwaukee. In many countries, people are also increasingly questioning definitive evidence on divisive issues such as vaccines, partly because scientific information is being drowned out online.

Researchers say this is a problem because it undermines support for urgent policies — such as ones that tackle climate change — and because it can lead to personal decisions that harm health, such as shunning vaccines or medical treatments. “When science rejection leads to loss of life, that’s concerning,” says Natalia Zarzeczna, who studies people’s beliefs at the University of Essex in Colchester, UK.

## Pandemic problems

Concerns about trust in science have simmered for years, but they exploded during the COVID-19 pandemic, when misinformation flourished and vocal groups questioned recommendations — such as vaccination and face masks — that research suggested could save lives.

How FAIR data are helping to build trust in science

In June 2022, as the pandemic waned, researchers Niels Mede and Viktoria Cologna put a call out on Twitter (now known as X) for people interested in surveying trust in science. Their tweets blew up — and before long they had a team of about 240 people, an international project called TISP (Trust in Science and Science-Related Populism) and [the 68-country survey](https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-024-00420-1). “It got quite some attention,” says Mede, who is now at Wageningen University & Research in the Netherlands and co-led the study with Cologna, now at the Swiss Federal Institute of Aquatic Science and Technology in Dübendorf.

The online survey asked 12 questions about scientists’ competence, integrity, openness and benevolence, which are different dimensions of trust. This aimed to address criticism that surveys about trust in science in general are simplistic, because [‘trust’ and ‘science’ are broad terms](https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-026-00467-2). The team combined the results into a scale of trustworthiness, from 1 (very low) to 5 (very high). The 3.6 global average largely fits with earlier global surveys suggesting that [trust in science is high](https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-024-00238-x) (see ‘Solid support for science’).

The TISP analysis showed some regional variation. Trust was relatively high in some African countries, including Nigeria and Kenya, and low in Russia and some nations that were part of the former Soviet Union, such as Kazakhstan. (Mede says that high trust in some places, such as certain African nations, might be because people view scientists more favourably than governments that are seen as corrupt.) The United States ranked in the top third, and China near the middle.

Source: Ipsos Global Trustworthiness index 2024.

Kathleen Hall Jamieson, a specialist in science communication at the University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia, argues that there’s “a rhetoric of science in crisis”, rather than an actual one — and that it’s nothing new. She traces the idea back to the widening recognition by scientists and the media in the 2010s, that many results in biomedicine and psychology could not be reproduced, a situation often portrayed as a ‘reproducibility crisis’.

But data and experts largely point in the same direction. “Scientists are still regarded as quite trustworthy,” sums up Eileen Yam, who directs science and society research at the Pew Research Center in Washington DC. Or at least, that’s “the glass half-full rendering”, she says.

## Fractures in trust

Source: General Social Survey.

“There are trend lines down in science, but those look very much like the trend lines in other institutions,” says Jamieson. “There’s an institutional crisis that is being reflected in science.”

Source: General Social Survey.

But that’s not the only explanation for the polarization in the United States: politicians have fuelled it, too. Gauchat says that, starting in the mid-1990s, some politicians “realized they could mobilize groups of people” in the United States who were becoming critical of higher education in part because of its high cost. They helped to power the populist view that scientists, other academics and their institutions are part of an intellectual elite, “making them the villains”, who do not represent the views of ordinary citizens, says Gauchat.

Scientists should recognize their own political biases to build public trust

The pandemic accelerated and amplified the partisan divergence, say researchers, as some people grew sceptical of regulations on COVID-19 vaccines, face masks, lockdowns and other measures that science suggested could limit infections, while politicians fanned the flames of science distrust. Jamieson argues that often people object to policies that stem from science rather than the science itself. “If your ideology says we shouldn’t be regulated, and the implication of the science is [that] politicians put regulation on the table, it’s going to be easy for people to say, ‘I don’t like that’,” she says.

The threat now, say researchers, is that the Trump administration is using science scepticism to justify drastic cuts to research and the [undermining of evidence-based interventions such as vaccines](https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-026-00088-9). “They’re saying, we’re going to destroy these things, because this whole institution is not trustworthy,” Druckman says.

From the United States to Europe to Brazil, there is a pervasive sense that trust in science has collapsed.
The complex truth about trust in science
A UK survey 1 published in January found that only 40% of people think that science information they hear is “generally true”. Another global poll showed that 70% of people believe at least one false or unproven claim, such as that the risks of childhood vaccines outweigh the benefits 2 .
In the United States, President Donald Trump and his administration are using the idea that science is not trustworthy as one reason to cut research budgets , reject evidence-based medical advice and exert unprecedented political control over research. “Over the last 5 years, confidence that scientists act in the best interests of the public has fallen significantly,” said Trump in an executive order last year .
Even the Vatican is voicing concern. This September, a meeting at the Pontifical Academy of Sciences will examine how “the crisis of trust in science has become a pressing issue”.
But is trust in science really that weak? Researchers studying this have reached some surprising conclusions. From a global perspective, public trust in science and scientists is high, they say. One of the largest studies 3 , which surveyed nearly 72,000 people across 68 countries in 2022–23, reported a “moderately high” average trust score of 3.6 out of 5. “The idea that there’s a generalized, pervasive lack of trust in science and experts is just completely unfounded in my mind,” says David Bersoff, head of research at the Edelman Trust Institute, a think tank in New York City.
Six ways to put the public at the heart of science and policy
But trust has dropped in certain groups, notably among Republican-leaning people in the United States. And research in the United Kingdom shows that the proportion of people who have “a lot” of trust in science tends to be lower among politically right-leaning groups than those on the left. “Trust in science is politicized and becoming more so,” says sociologist Gordon Gauchat at the University of Wisconsin–Milwaukee. In many countries, people are also increasingly questioning definitive evidence on divisive issues such as vaccines, partly because scientific information is being drowned out online.
Researchers say this is a problem because it undermines support for urgent policies — such as ones that tackle climate change — and because it can lead to personal decisions that harm health, such as shunning vaccines or medical treatments. “When science rejection leads to loss of life, that’s concerning,” says Natalia Zarzeczna, who studies people’s beliefs at the University of Essex in Colchester, UK.

The United States ranked in the top third, and China near the middle.
Other data show that trust in scientists is high relative to that in other professions. A 28-country survey 4 run by the Edelman Trust Institute in 2025 found that 76% of respondents trusted scientists, a proportion on a par with teachers (73%) and well above that for journalists (54%) and government leaders (49%). “Probably a lot of other sectors and professions would like to be in science’s shoes,” says Gideon Skinner, head of political research at market-research firm Ipsos in London, which has conducted international surveys that also show scientists in the top tier of trusted professions (see ‘Trust in professions’).
Source: Ipsos Global Trustworthiness index 2024.
Kathleen Hall Jamieson, a specialist in science communication at the University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia, argues that there’s “a rhetoric of science in crisis”, rather than an actual one — and that it’s nothing new. The glass half-empty view, however, has data to support it, too. In a survey of people living in Britain, published in April 5 , 84% of respondents said they had at least some trust in science. But the proportion who trusted science “a lot” dropped from 63% in 2020 to 34% — one of the “emerging fractures” in trust that the study identified.
One of the most prominent changes is taking place in the United States. Here, data collected by the General Social Survey (GSS) from 1973 to 2024 show that, overall, the proportion of people with some or a great deal of confidence in the scientific community remained stably high (above 80%) over 50 years 6 . But the proportion with a great deal of confidence declined sharply in 2022 (see ‘US confidence in science’).
Source: General Social Survey.
This drop is part of a wider loss of trust in civic institutions, rather than being unique to science, research indicates 7 . A survey 8 by the Pew Research Center shows that the proportion of people with confidence in scientists to act in the public’s interest fell from 87% in 2020 to 73% in 2023. But confidence in police officers, business leaders and elected officials similarly fell over this time.

從美國、歐洲到巴西，一種普遍的感受是：人們對科學的信任已經崩塌。

關於科學信任的複雜真相

在美國，總統唐納・川普（Donald Trump）及其政府正把「科學不可信」這個說法，當作[削減研究預算](https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-026-00088-9)、[否定以證據為基礎的醫療建議](https://www.nature.com/articles/d41591-026-00002-w)，並對研究施加前所未有政治控制的理由之一。川普在[去年的一項行政命令](https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2025/05/restoring-gold-standard-science/)中表示：「過去 5 年來，民眾相信科學家會以公共利益為優先的信心已大幅下降。」

連梵蒂岡也表達了憂慮。今年 9 月，宗座科學院將召開會議，探討「科學信任危機如何成為迫切議題」。

讓公眾成為科學與政策核心的六種方法

但在某些群體中，信任已經下降，特別是在美國傾向支持共和黨的人之間。英國的研究也顯示，政治立場偏右的群體中，對科學抱有「高度」信任的人口比例，往往低於左派群體。「對科學的信任已經政治化，而且程度越來越高，」威斯康辛大學密爾瓦基分校的社會學家 Gordon Gauchat 說。在許多國家，人們也越來越常質疑分歧性議題上的明確證據，例如疫苗；部分原因是科學資訊在網路上被其他聲量淹沒。

研究人員說，這是個問題，因為它會削弱對緊急政策的支持，例如因應氣候變遷的政策；也可能導致傷害健康的個人決定，例如避開疫苗或醫療治療。「當拒斥科學導致生命損失時，那就令人擔憂，」研究人們信念的 Natalia Zarzeczna 說。她任職於英國科爾切斯特的艾塞克斯大學。

## 疫情難題

對科學信任的憂慮已經醞釀多年，但在 COVID-19 疫情期間爆發開來；當時錯誤資訊氾濫，也有高聲量群體質疑研究顯示可能挽救生命的建議，例如接種疫苗與戴口罩。

FAIR 資料如何協助建立對科學的信任

2022 年 6 月，隨著疫情趨緩，研究人員 Niels Mede 和 Viktoria Cologna 在 Twitter（現稱 X）上發文，徵求有興趣參與科學信任調查的人。他們的推文引起熱烈迴響，不久後便組成了一個約 240 人的團隊，成立名為 TISP（Trust in Science and Science-Related Populism，對科學的信任與科學相關民粹主義）的國際計畫，並完成了[涵蓋 68 國的調查](https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-024-00420-1)。「這引起了不少關注，」Mede 說。他現在任職於荷蘭瓦赫寧恩大學暨研究中心，並與 Cologna 共同主導這項研究；Cologna 目前任職於瑞士杜本多夫的瑞士聯邦水科學與技術研究所。

線上調查詢問了 12 個關於科學家能力、誠信、開放性與善意的問題，這些都是信任的不同面向。這是為了回應外界批評：一般談科學信任的調查往往過於簡化，因為[「信任」與「科學」都是範圍很廣的詞](https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-026-00467-2)。研究團隊將結果整合成一個可信賴程度量表，從 1（非常低）到 5（非常高）。全球平均 3.6 分大致符合先前全球調查的結果，也就是[大眾對科學的信任度很高](https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-024-00238-x)（見「對科學的穩固支持」）。

TISP 分析顯示，不同地區之間有些差異。部分非洲國家的信任度相對較高，包括奈及利亞與肯亞；俄羅斯以及一些曾屬前蘇聯的國家，例如哈薩克，信任度則偏低。（Mede 表示，某些地方的高信任度，例如部分非洲國家，可能是因為人們相較於被視為貪腐的政府，對科學家的觀感更好。）美國排名落在前段三分之一，中國則接近中段。

資料來源：Ipsos Global Trustworthiness index 2024。

賓州大學（University of Pennsylvania）位於費城的科學傳播專家 Kathleen Hall Jamieson 主張，所謂「科學陷入危機」比較像是一種說法，而不是真正的危機，而且這也不是什麼新現象。她將這個想法追溯到 2010 年代，當時科學家與媒體越來越意識到，生物醫學與心理學的許多研究結果無法重現，這種狀況常被描繪成「可重現性危機」。

但資料與專家看法大致指向同一個方向。華盛頓特區皮尤研究中心（Pew Research Center）負責科學與社會研究的 Eileen Yam 總結說：「科學家仍然被視為相當值得信任。」或者至少，她說，這是「把杯子看成半滿」的說法。

## 信任的裂痕

資料來源：General Social Survey。

Jamieson 說：「科學領域確實有一些趨勢線往下走，但那些趨勢線看起來和其他機構的趨勢線非常相似。這是一場機構危機，而它也反映在科學上。」

資料來源：General Social Survey。

但這不是美國社會兩極化的唯一解釋：政治人物也推波助瀾。Gauchat 說，從 1990 年代中期開始，有些政治人物「意識到自己可以動員一群人」，這些人在美國開始批判高等教育，部分原因是學費高昂。他們助長了一種民粹觀點，認為科學家、其他學者及其機構都是知識菁英的一部分，「把他們塑造成反派」，而且不代表一般公民的看法，Gauchat 說。

科學家應該認清自身的政治偏見，以建立公眾信任

研究人員表示，疫情加速並放大了黨派分歧：有些人開始懷疑 COVID-19 疫苗、口罩、封城與其他科學指出可限制感染的措施，而政治人物則煽動對科學的不信任。Jamieson 主張，人們反對的往往是源自科學的政策，而不是科學本身。她說：「如果你的意識形態認為我們不應該受到管制，而科學所帶出的含意是政治人物把管制擺上檯面，那麼人們就很容易說：『我不喜歡那樣。』」

研究人員表示，現在的威脅是，川普政府正在利用科學懷疑論，為大幅削減研究經費，以及[削弱疫苗等以證據為基礎的介入措施](https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-026-00088-9)尋找正當性。Druckman 說：「他們的說法是，我們要摧毀這些東西，因為這整個制度都不值得信任。」

插圖：Nik Spencer／*Nature*。改編自 Accogliente Design／Shutterstock 的圖片

從美國、歐洲到巴西，一種普遍的感受是：人們對科學的信任已經崩塌。

關於科學信任的複雜真相

在美國，總統唐納・川普（Donald Trump）及其政府正把「科學不可信」這個說法，當作[削減研究預算](https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-026-00088-9)、[否定以證據為基礎的醫療建議](https://www.nature.com/articles/d41591-026-00002-w)，並對研究施加前所未有政治控制的理由之一。川普在[去年的一項行政命令](https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2025/05/restoring-gold-standard-science/)中表示：「過去 5 年來，民眾相信科學家會以公共利益為優先的信心已大幅下降。」

連梵蒂岡也表達了憂慮。今年 9 月，宗座科學院將召開會議，探討「科學信任危機如何成為迫切議題」。

讓公眾成為科學與政策核心的六種方法

但在某些群體中，信任已經下降，特別是在美國傾向支持共和黨的人之間。英國的研究也顯示，政治立場偏右的群體中，對科學抱有「高度」信任的人口比例，往往低於左派群體。「對科學的信任已經政治化，而且程度越來越高，」威斯康辛大學密爾瓦基分校的社會學家 Gordon Gauchat 說。在許多國家，人們也越來越常質疑分歧性議題上的明確證據，例如疫苗；部分原因是科學資訊在網路上被其他聲量淹沒。

研究人員說，這是個問題，因為它會削弱對緊急政策的支持，例如因應氣候變遷的政策；也可能導致傷害健康的個人決定，例如避開疫苗或醫療治療。「當拒斥科學導致生命損失時，那就令人擔憂，」研究人們信念的 Natalia Zarzeczna 說。她任職於英國科爾切斯特的艾塞克斯大學。

## 疫情難題

對科學信任的憂慮已經醞釀多年，但在 COVID-19 疫情期間爆發開來；當時錯誤資訊氾濫，也有高聲量群體質疑研究顯示可能挽救生命的建議，例如接種疫苗與戴口罩。

FAIR 資料如何協助建立對科學的信任

2022 年 6 月，隨著疫情趨緩，研究人員 Niels Mede 和 Viktoria Cologna 在 Twitter（現稱 X）上發文，徵求有興趣參與科學信任調查的人。他們的推文引起熱烈迴響，不久後便組成了一個約 240 人的團隊，成立名為 TISP（Trust in Science and Science-Related Populism，對科學的信任與科學相關民粹主義）的國際計畫，並完成了[涵蓋 68 國的調查](https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-024-00420-1)。「這引起了不少關注，」Mede 說。他現在任職於荷蘭瓦赫寧恩大學暨研究中心，並與 Cologna 共同主導這項研究；Cologna 目前任職於瑞士杜本多夫的瑞士聯邦水科學與技術研究所。

線上調查詢問了 12 個關於科學家能力、誠信、開放性與善意的問題，這些都是信任的不同面向。這是為了回應外界批評：一般談科學信任的調查往往過於簡化，因為[「信任」與「科學」都是範圍很廣的詞](https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-026-00467-2)。研究團隊將結果整合成一個可信賴程度量表，從 1（非常低）到 5（非常高）。全球平均 3.6 分大致符合先前全球調查的結果，也就是[大眾對科學的信任度很高](https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-024-00238-x)（見「對科學的穩固支持」）。

TISP 分析顯示，不同地區之間有些差異。部分非洲國家的信任度相對較高，包括奈及利亞與肯亞；俄羅斯以及一些曾屬前蘇聯的國家，例如哈薩克，信任度則偏低。（Mede 表示，某些地方的高信任度，例如部分非洲國家，可能是因為人們相較於被視為貪腐的政府，對科學家的觀感更好。）美國排名落在前段三分之一，中國則接近中段。

資料來源：Ipsos Global Trustworthiness index 2024。

賓州大學（University of Pennsylvania）位於費城的科學傳播專家 Kathleen Hall Jamieson 主張，所謂「科學陷入危機」比較像是一種說法，而不是真正的危機，而且這也不是什麼新現象。她將這個想法追溯到 2010 年代，當時科學家與媒體越來越意識到，生物醫學與心理學的許多研究結果無法重現，這種狀況常被描繪成「可重現性危機」。

但資料與專家看法大致指向同一個方向。華盛頓特區皮尤研究中心（Pew Research Center）負責科學與社會研究的 Eileen Yam 總結說：「科學家仍然被視為相當值得信任。」或者至少，她說，這是「把杯子看成半滿」的說法。

## 信任的裂痕

資料來源：General Social Survey。

Jamieson 說：「科學領域確實有一些趨勢線往下走，但那些趨勢線看起來和其他機構的趨勢線非常相似。這是一場機構危機，而它也反映在科學上。」

資料來源：General Social Survey。

但這不是美國社會兩極化的唯一解釋：政治人物也推波助瀾。Gauchat 說，從 1990 年代中期開始，有些政治人物「意識到自己可以動員一群人」，這些人在美國開始批判高等教育，部分原因是學費高昂。他們助長了一種民粹觀點，認為科學家、其他學者及其機構都是知識菁英的一部分，「把他們塑造成反派」，而且不代表一般公民的看法，Gauchat 說。

科學家應該認清自身的政治偏見，以建立公眾信任

研究人員表示，疫情加速並放大了黨派分歧：有些人開始懷疑 COVID-19 疫苗、口罩、封城與其他科學指出可限制感染的措施，而政治人物則煽動對科學的不信任。Jamieson 主張，人們反對的往往是源自科學的政策，而不是科學本身。她說：「如果你的意識形態認為我們不應該受到管制，而科學所帶出的含意是政治人物把管制擺上檯面，那麼人們就很容易說：『我不喜歡那樣。』」

研究人員表示，現在的威脅是，川普政府正在利用科學懷疑論，為大幅削減研究經費，以及[削弱疫苗等以證據為基礎的介入措施](https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-026-00088-9)尋找正當性。Druckman 說：「他們的說法是，我們要摧毀這些東西，因為這整個制度都不值得信任。」
